name: Bambam
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_quote: Stress in PUS is not phonemic. It normally occurs on the penultimate syllable of words or on the nucleus of the rare one-syllable roots. The addition of any suffixes to the word (thus making a new word) affects the placement of stress; that is, it causes the stress to shift to the right.

audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed penultimate, word domain excluding clitics) rests on the best and only dedicated phonology of the language, Campbell 1991 (SIL WILC 12, 52 pp), written by the resident fieldworker; the deciding quotation was verified verbatim at printed p.11 §3.1 of the PDF we hold, and the same statement appears in the held 1989 MA thesis §2.2 p.15. Campbell's qualifications (vocatives final-stressed; enclitics outside the stress domain; suffixes shift stress rightward, i.e. penult of the suffixed word) are consistent with the 'fixed-strict' penult rule string and the word domain note already in the domain locator. Glottolog lists no other grammar/phonology and a web search found no newer instrumental or descriptive study, so no better source exists to hold; nothing open was available to download (Smith 1993 is comparative and its MPG PuRe PDF is access-restricted). tone.quote: 3. SUPRA SEGMENTAL CONSIDERATIONS 3.1 Stress Stress in PUS is not phonemic. It normally occurs on the penultimate syllable of words or on the nucleus of the rare one-syllable roots. The addition of any suffixes to the word (thus making a new word) affects the placement of stress; that is, it causes the stress to shift to the right. [...] 3.2 Intonation 3.2.1 Sentence Level Intonation Generally, PUS questions end with nsmg [sic, scanned: rising] intonation which begins on the stressed syllable of the last word. This applies both to content questions and yes-no questions. Statements and imperatives have falling intonation.

tone.quote: 2.2 Stress Stress in PUS is not phonemic. It normally occurs on the penultimate syllable of words or on the nucleus of the rare one-syllable roots. The addition of any suffixes to the word (thus making a new word) affects the placement of stress; that is, it causes the stress to shift to the right. [...] In addition to the changes described above, there are also suprasegmental changes. The stress on the penultimate syllable is noticeably stronger and the stressed vowel is pronounced with a correspondingly higher pitch.
